parts.text: Natural English: “Thank you for this morning! I was surprised by how good your Japanese is! I look forward to getting to know you / keeping in touch!” Her use of hiragana may make the message easier for a learner to read, but the reason for that spelling is unknown.

こちらこそ、今朝はありがとうございました！

日本語はまだまだですが、そう言ってもらえてうれしいです！英語もとても上手ですね！

お会いできてうれしかったです。これからもよろしくお願いします！

実は、日本語を読んだり書いたりするとき、翻訳や文章を考えるのにChatGPTに手伝ってもらっています。意味や文法をもっとよく理解するためにも使っています。漢字も勉強中です！

こんなに長い文章は、まだ何も見ずに話せません！笑

そういえば、さっき出てこなかった言葉は「看護師」でした！昔は看護師をしていたんですが、今は家で子どもの世話をしています。

Thank you too for this morning!

My Japanese still has a long way to go, but I'm happy you said that! Your English is very good too!

It was lovely to meet you. I look forward to keeping in touch!

Actually, when reading or writing Japanese I use ChatGPT to help translate and work out what to write. I also use it to understand meanings and grammar better. I'm learning kanji too!

I still couldn't speak something this long without looking at anything! Haha.

Oh, by the way, the word I couldn't think of earlier was “nurse”! I used to work as a nurse, but these days I stay at home and look after the children.

Register: friendly polite Japanese (です／ます) suited to a new acquaintance. こちらこそ responds to thanks; まだまだ modestly accepts a compliment; これからもよろしくお願いします reciprocates an invitation to future contact. The later そういえば returns to a forgotten word from the in-person conversation.

A shorter version for spontaneous speech: 「日本語はまだまだです。話すときは、こんなに長く話せません（笑）。」 (“My Japanese still has a long way to go. I can't speak at this length when talking!”). Try saying it aloud without reading, then replace 「こんなに長く」 with 「上手に」 (well) or 「速く」 (quickly).
けさはありがとうございました！ = “Thank you for this morning.” 今朝 is a whole-word reading, “this morning”. ありがとうございました uses the past polite thank-you form for an earlier event.

にほんごがとてもじょうずでおどろきました！ = “I was surprised by how good your Japanese is!” 日本語が = Japanese (as the subject of the assessment); とても = very; 上手 = skilled/good at; で = connecting form of the な-adjective 上手だ, giving the reason/background for 驚きました = “I was surprised”. This で is not a place marker here.

これからよろしくおねがいします！ これから = “from now on / going forward”; よろしくお願いします expresses goodwill about an ongoing relationship. In this context it is closer to “I look forward to keeping in touch” than merely “nice to meet you”. With これからも in the reply, も adds “also / continuing from here”.

こちらこそ = “likewise / thank you too”. 日本語はまだまだですが = “my Japanese still has a long way to go, but…”; まだまだ is conventional modesty without completely rejecting the compliment. そう言ってもらえてうれしいです literally presents the nice words as a benefit received: 言う → 言って → 言ってもらう → 言ってもらえる → 言ってもらえて; “I'm happy you said that.” 英語もとても上手ですね returns the compliment politely.

お会いできてうれしかったです = “I was happy to meet you.” The polite humble pattern お + 会い (verb stem) + できる conveys being able to meet the person. できて joins to うれしかったです (past of うれしいです). More everyday and simpler: 会えてうれしかったです.

実は = “actually”. 日本語を読んだり書いたりするとき = “when doing things such as reading and writing Japanese”. The pattern 〜たり〜たりする lists example activities without implying order: 読む → 読んだ → 読んだり, 書く → 書いた → 書いたり. Compare 読んで書く, which more directly chains two actions.

翻訳や文章を考えるのにChatGPTに手伝ってもらっています = “I use ChatGPT's help for translation and working out written sentences”. や lists examples; 〜のに here marks what help is *for*; ChatGPTに identifies the helper; 手伝ってもらう means to receive help; 〜ています describes the regular situation. 意味や文法をもっとよく理解するためにも使っています = “I also use it to understand meanings and grammar better”. 〜ために expresses purpose; the も adds another purpose.
漢字も勉強中です = “I'm studying kanji too.” The suffix 〜中 indicates that something is in progress, as in 仕事中 “working” or 練習中 “practising”.

こんなに長い文章は、まだ何も見ずに話せません！笑 = “I still can't say something this long without looking at anything! Haha.” こんなに = “this much”; 〜ずに = “without doing” (見ない → 見ずに); 話す → 話せる → 話せません is polite negative potential (“can't speak/say”). This wording emphasises reliance on a written prompt. （笑） or 笑 often signals a lighthearted laugh in chat.

看護師= nurse (professional title). The word did not come to mind during the in-person conversation, and I clarified it in my reply.

そういえば = “oh, by the way / come to think of it”. さっき = “a little earlier”. 出てこなかった言葉 = “the word that wouldn't come to mind”. This is idiomatic: 言葉が出てこない (“I can't think of the word”) works in any future conversation. Past negative: 出てくる → 出てこない → 出てこなかった.

昔は看護師をしていたんですが、今は家で子どもの世話をしています。 = “I used to work as a nurse, but now I look after the children at home.” 昔は contrasts previous life with 今は. 〜をしていた describes a past occupation. 〜んですが gently supplies explanatory background and contrast. 家で gives the place of activity; 子どもの世話をする means to care for children.

parts.text:
Natural English translation

“Even kanji! I'm studying English using Gemini and apps too, but when I actually speak with someone I get nervous, and because I don't feel I've studied enough, my mind goes blank. 😭 So seeing you speak that much Japanese straight away made me feel that you must have studied really hard. I admire you! What inspired you to start learning Japanese?

Oh, so you used to be a nurse! And you have a daughter too! ✨ My husband's overseas assignment was confirmed, so I left my job sourcing electronic components and moved here from Japan in August!”

English meaning

Yes, I love kanji! They're like difficult picture puzzles. I don't think I'll ever remember them all (haha), but I love how beautiful they look. My daughter Evie likes writing kanji too, and we sometimes write them together. When I see the same kanji many times, I gradually remember their meanings.

It's normal to feel nervous when speaking a foreign language, isn't it? I get nervous too! I'm sure you've studied a lot. But studying and actually speaking are completely different, aren't they? I speak with the attitude that it's okay to make mistakes. Sometimes funny things happen when I make mistakes (haha). I learn a lot from my mistakes.

I made some Japanese friends at university and started studying Japanese. Spending time with them was really fun. I'd already liked Japanese culture before that. Now learning foreign languages is a hobby I want to continue for the rest of my life.

Welcome to Oxford! I imagine moving was difficult. Have you got a little more used to life in Britain?

In a real conversation: いざ〜と / 〜てしまう

いざ人と話すと = “when it comes to actually talking with someone.” The いざ marks the moment theory becomes reality; 〜と introduces what happens when that condition occurs. 緊張と勉強不足で = “because of nerves and not having studied enough.”

何も出てこなくなってしまいます has several layers: 出てくる (come out / come to mind) → 出てこない (does not come out) → 出てこなくなる (become unable to bring it to mind) → 出てこなくなってしまう (unfortunately end up that way). The 〜てしまう expresses an unwelcome outcome. This is about language retrieval under pressure, not literally losing everything she has learned.

Complimenting and inferring: 話せる / だろうな / されてる

話す → 話せる is the potential (“can speak”). 相当勉強されてるんだろうなと感じました roughly means “I felt you must have studied quite a lot.” The respectful されてる refers to your studying (short for されている). The だろうな expresses an impression or guess, and と感じました reports what she thought. 尊敬します is “I admire/respect you.” She is impressed by your spontaneous effort, not declaring that you are fluent.

Asking about motivation: 〜ようと思ったきっかけ

日本語を学ぼうと思ったきっかけは何ですか？ = “What prompted you to want to learn Japanese?” 学ぶ → 学ぼう is the volitional form (“I'll learn”); と思った expresses the intention/decision; きっかけ is the reason, event or experience that prompted it. Compare 日本語を勉強しようと思ったきっかけ (“what prompted you to decide to study Japanese?”). This is an invitation to share a personal story.

Acknowledging news and explaining a move

看護師さんだったんですね (“Oh, so you were a nurse!”) and 娘さんもいらっしゃるんですね (“And you have a daughter!”) show she has taken in your earlier reply. The 〜んですね sounds interested and responsive; いらっしゃる is polite language for having someone here.

夫の海外出向が決まり describes her husband's overseas posting being confirmed. 電子部品調達の仕事を辞めて says she left her procurement job. 8月に日本から引っ越してきました = she moved here from Japan in August; 〜てきました views the movement toward the present location.

parts.text:
Style and tone

The response uses friendly です／ます speech rather than stiff formal language. 「私も緊張します」 makes reassurance reciprocal, 「ですよね」 invites agreement, 「と思います」 softens judgements, and （笑） keeps the two jokes light. The story about Evie gives the exchange a personal detail. 「きっとたくさん勉強されていると思います」 is a respectful acknowledgement, not a claim to know how much someone has studied.

2 · Liking an activity, habits, and linking descriptions

娘のエヴィも漢字を書くのが好きです。 — “Evie also likes writing kanji.” With V dictionary form＋のが好き, の turns the activity into a noun-like phrase: compare 「漢字が好き」 (likes kanji) with 「漢字を書くのが好き」 (likes *writing* kanji).

For い-adjectives use 〜くて: 楽しい → 楽しくて. Don't confuse this で with location-marking で (家で) or means-marking で (日本語で).

3 · When, if, repetition and gradual results

同じ漢字を何度も見ると、少しずつ意味を覚えます。 — “When I see the same kanji repeatedly, I gradually remember the meaning.” 何度も = many times; 少しずつ = little by little. Vると often describes a natural, habitual or predictable result. Vるとき means *when doing* something, not necessarily cause-and-effect. Compare 時間があったら、一緒に行きましょう for a possible future condition plus an invitation: 〜たら is more flexible here than 〜と.

外国語で話すとき — “when speaking in a foreign language.” The で is a means/language marker; 話すとき is a time clause. It isn't the same construction as 話すと、… meaning “when/if you speak, [result]”.

4 · Talking about nerves and inviting agreement

緊張するのは普通ですよね。 — “Being nervous is normal, isn't it?” Vる＋の turns “being nervous” into a topic; は marks it; 普通 is the description. ですよね invites the listener to agree from shared experience. 「私も緊張します」 (“I get nervous too”) expresses solidarity without claiming to know how Mayumi feels.

勉強するのと実際に話すのは全然違いますよね。 — “Studying and actually speaking are completely different, aren't they?” Here two nominalised actions are compared with と. 全然＋違う is natural and strong; 全然 often pairs with negative expressions but can occur with positive ones colloquially.

きっとたくさん勉強されていると思います expresses a kind inference about her effort. されている is respectful speech for what she does, not the passive 'is being studied' here. Compare the simpler 「たくさん勉強していると思います」 when speaking about a close friend rather than politely addressing someone.

5 · 'It's okay to…', learning from mistakes, and possible outcomes

間違えてもいい！ — “It's okay to make mistakes!” Vて＋もいい gives permission or acceptance; with です it becomes a polite statement, and 〜てもいいですか asks permission. This differs from 〜てはいけません, “mustn't do it”. 私は『間違えてもいい！』と思って話しています means “I speak with the attitude that mistakes are okay”; と思って describes the thought guiding your behaviour.

間違えると、面白いこともあります — “Sometimes funny things happen when I make mistakes.” こともあります means *there are also occasions when…*; it doesn't mean mistakes are always funny. 間違いからよく学びます uses から to identify the source of learning, as with 人から学ぶ (learn from a person). Not all から examples mean “because”: 失敗から学ぶ is “learn from failure”, whereas 疲れたから休みます is “I'll rest because I'm tired”.

6 · Making friends, starting something, and recalling an earlier interest

大学で日本人の友達ができて、日本語を勉強し始めました。 — “I made Japanese friends at university and started learning Japanese.” 友達ができる is a set phrase meaning *make friends / gain a friend*. It is not identical to 日本語ができる (“can use Japanese”). The て-form in できて links it to what followed; it does not automatically say the activities happened simultaneously. 勉強し始める = 勉強する → 勉強します → 勉強し＋始める; with a plain verb, 読む → 読み始める.

一緒にいるのがとても楽しかったです — “Being together was really fun.” Again Vる＋のが, but now followed by 楽しかったです rather than 好き. 前から日本の文化も好きでした = “I'd liked Japanese culture since before.” 前から is vague; it doesn't specify an exact start date. 今では contrasts now with the past. ずっと続けたい趣味 = “a hobby I want to keep up for a long time”; Vます-stem＋たい expresses the speaker's wish, and the clause modifies 趣味.

7 · A friendly welcome and gentle questions

オックスフォードへようこそ！ — “Welcome to Oxford!” へ marks a destination; this is a fixed and friendly welcome. 引っ越しは大変だったと思います — “I imagine the move was difficult.” 大変だった is past tense of the な-adjective 大変だ; と思います makes this your inference rather than an assertion about someone else's experience. A more neutral option is 引っ越しはどうでしたか？ (“How was the move?”).

イギリスの生活には少し慣れましたか？ — “Have you got a little used to life in Britain?” N＋に慣れる = become accustomed to something. には highlights that topic: “As for life in Britain…”. 慣れてきました can mean “I've gradually started getting used to it.” When the thing being got used to is an action, use Vる＋のに慣れる: 早く起きるのに慣れました (“I've got used to getting up early”). Here のに is nominalisation＋に, not the adversative のに meaning “although”.

Practice: a natural Japanese conversation about hobbies, music and playing piano. We worked on 〜たり〜たりする, 〜のが好き／〜ことが好き, 〜や／〜とか, 〜から, 〜と思います and 〜やすい. The long original below was written with time and care, not produced spontaneously. Future practice should develop quicker, shorter responses and build complexity gradually rather than memorising the full answer.

My original Japanese (carefully composed; retain exactly):

ロックやジャズが大好きなんだけど、クラシックとかレゲエ、エレクトロニカとか、他にもいろんなジャンルの音楽を聴くよ。それぞれ違う良さがあって、心に響くものがあるから、幅広い音楽が好きなんだよね。

Natural English: “I love rock and jazz, but I also listen to classical, reggae, electronica and all sorts of other genres. Each has something different to offer, something that resonates with me, so I enjoy a wide variety of music.” The original is fluent-sounding, informal Japanese; its preparation time matters when choosing subsequent speaking exercises.

Understanding the long answer:

や (“and things like…”) and とか (“such as…”) list examples rather than all possibilities. なんだけど combines informal explanation (んだ) with けど (“but…”) to open out the thought; 聴くよ and 好きなんだよね are conversational endings. それぞれ違う良さがあって means each has its own particular appeal; あって links to the next clause. 心に響く means emotionally resonates or moves the listener. 〜から gives the reason for liking many genres. The sentence naturally uses casual Japanese; with a new acquaintance, consider です／ます.

Shorter *new* example for speaking without preparation: 「ロックとジャズが好きです。でも、ほかの音楽も聴きます。それぞれ良さがあるからです。」

First spontaneous activity-listing attempt: 「ピアノを惹くたり聴くたりしま。」

Corrected: 「ピアノを弾いたり、音楽を聴いたりします。」 (“I do things like playing piano and listening to music.”)

弾く = play an instrument; 聴く = listen attentively; 惹く = attract. For 〜たり, take the plain past form plus り: 弾く → 弾いた → 弾いたり; 聴く → 聴いた → 聴いたり. Finish with します. The natural objects are ピアノを弾く and 音楽を聴く. The たり pattern lists examples, not events in sequence.

Other learner-authored sentences:

「Yann tiersen と einaudi を聴くことが大好きです。」 — “I love listening to Yann Tiersen and Einaudi.” 〜ことが好き is correct; 〜のが好き is another especially conversational option. Listening = 聴く, playing = 弾く. Contrast 「二人の曲を聴くのが好きです。」 and 「二人の曲をピアノで弾くのが好きです。」

Question asked: 「その二人の曲を、ピアノでも弾きますか？」 (“Do you also play their pieces on piano?”)

Actual reply: 「はい、彼らの音楽は覚えやすいと思います。ゆっくりと穏やかです。」 — “Yes. I think their music is easy to remember. It is slow and calm.” The はい ALREADY clearly answers yes; Japanese naturally omits a repeated predicate when understood. Do not criticise this as an unanswered question. 覚えやすい = easy to remember; 弾きやすい = easy to play. Optional stylistic alternative, not a required correction: 「テンポがゆっくりで、穏やかな曲が多いです。」

parts.text:
漢字大好きなんですね〜！✨子供と一緒に楽しんで覚えるのとてもいいですね！エヴィちゃんは何歳ですか？

本当にその通りな上にとても素晴らしい考えで見習いたいです！✨今日Jonさんに話しかけるのもかなり緊張してたのですが、勇気出して良かったとしみじみ思っています🥺

そういうきっかけがあったんですね！日本が好きって言ってもらえるとなんだか嬉しいです☺️外国語の勉強が趣味ってすごいですね！！

ありがとうございます！最初はホームシックでしたが、今はだいぶ慣れました！景色がどこも綺麗で人も優しくてすごく良いところだと思ってます！

1. “Oh, you really love kanji! It's lovely that you and your child have fun learning them together. How old is Evie?”

2. “That's absolutely right, and such a wonderful outlook — I'd love to follow your example! I was quite nervous about approaching you today, but I'm genuinely glad I found the courage to do it.”

3. “Oh, so that's what inspired you! Somehow it makes me happy when someone says they like Japan. Studying foreign languages as a hobby — that's amazing!”

4. “Thank you! I was homesick at first, but I've got quite used to living here now. The scenery is beautiful everywhere and people are kind — I think it's a lovely place!”

Kanji and Evie

漢字大好きなんですね〜！ — “Oh, so you love kanji!” 〜なんですね shows interest in a newly learned fact. Compare 漢字が大好きです (“I love kanji”) with 漢字が大好きなんですね (“Oh, so you love kanji!”).

子供と一緒に楽しんで覚えるのとてもいいですね！ — “It's lovely to learn together with your child while having fun.” 子供と = with your child; 一緒に = together; 楽しんで = having fun (て-form of 楽しむ); 覚える = learn or memorise; の makes the whole activity something she can comment on. More fully: 覚えるのはとてもいいですね. エヴィちゃんは何歳ですか？ asks Evie's age; ちゃん is warm and affectionate.

Agreeing, complimenting and finding courage

本当にその通りな上に = “Exactly right, and on top of that…” その通り = just as you said; 〜上に adds another point. 素晴らしい考え = wonderful way of thinking; 見習いたい (見習う → 見習いたい) = want to follow someone's example.

今日Jonさんに話しかけるのもかなり緊張してたのですが = “Even approaching you today made me quite nervous, but…” 話しかける = initiate conversation (not merely 話す); かなり = considerably; 緊張してた = conversational contraction of 緊張していた; のも treats initiating the conversation as an activity and も adds “too/even.”

勇気出して良かったとしみじみ思っています = “I genuinely feel so glad I found the courage.” 勇気を出す = summon courage (を omitted colloquially); 〜て良かった = glad to have done something; しみじみ = deeply / reflectively; と marks the thought quoted before 思っています. This is heartfelt reflection, not simply polite thanks.

Responding to inspiration and kind words

そういうきっかけがあったんですね！ = “Oh, so that was your inspiration!” きっかけ = starting point or trigger; んですね signals interested acknowledgement.

日本が好きって言ってもらえるとなんだか嬉しいです = “Somehow it makes me happy when someone says they like Japan.” って is informal quotation (≈ と); 言ってもらえる = to have someone say something for one's benefit, potential of 言ってもらう; 〜と marks a natural/habitual result; なんだか = somehow, for some reason.

外国語の勉強が趣味ってすごいですね！！ = “Studying foreign languages as a hobby — that's impressive!” Here って introduces the whole idea being reacted to.

Settling into a new place

最初はホームシックでしたが、今はだいぶ慣れました！ = “I was homesick at first, but I've got quite used to it now!” 最初は / 今は contrast then and now; だいぶ = considerably; 慣れる = get accustomed to. With a specific target: 〜に慣れる, e.g. 新しい生活に慣れました.

景色がどこも綺麗で人も優しくて = “The scenery is beautiful everywhere and people are kind.” 綺麗 is a な-adjective, joined with で; 優しい is an い-adjective, joined with くて. すごく良いところだと思ってます = “I think it's a really good place”; 思ってます contracts 思っています. Her wording conveys that she has settled in more, not that she never misses home.

Responding naturally: 〜んですね and 〜上に

日本から引っ越してきたんですね！ — “Oh, so you moved here from Japan!” ピアノも弾くんですね！ — “Oh, you play piano too!” With nouns or な-adjectives, なんですね is common: 漢字が大好きなんですね.

〜上に adds a further point: この町は静かな上に便利です (“This town is quiet and convenient as well”). 日本語は面白い上に、勉強になります (“Japanese is interesting and educational too”). な-adjectives generally take な上に; い-adjectives attach directly to 上に.

Relief and reflection: 〜て良かった, 勇気を出す, しみじみ

話しかけて良かったです — “I'm glad I approached you.” 勇気を出して話しました — “I found the courage to speak.” 思い切って質問して良かったです — “I'm glad I took the plunge and asked.” 〜て良かった evaluates an action positively; compare 行って良かった (“I'm glad I went”) and 行けば良かった (“I wish I'd gone”).

しみじみ思う adds heartfelt reflection: 日本に来て良かったとしみじみ思います (“I feel deeply glad I came to Japan”). It's not required in everyday expressions of relief.

Quoted speech, receiving kindness and its effect: って / 〜てもらえると / なんだか

日本が好きって言ってくれました — “They told me they like Japan.” 日本が好きって言ってもらえると嬉しいです — “When someone says they like Japan, it makes me happy.” 褒めてもらえると嬉しいです — “I feel happy when someone praises me.” 手伝ってもらえると助かります — “It helps when someone lends a hand.”

なんだか = “somehow”: この曲を聴くと、なんだか落ち着きます (“Listening to this piece somehow calms me down”). The 〜と here signals a normal/predictable result.

Getting used to things and linking adjectives

〜に慣れる: 新しい学校に慣れてきました (“I'm gradually getting used to the new school”). 日本語で話すことにまだ慣れていません (“I'm not yet used to speaking Japanese”). 生活にだいぶ慣れました (“I've quite got used to life/the routine”). 〜てきました emphasises a developing change up to now.

Join descriptive clauses: このカフェは静かで、居心地がいいです (“This café is quiet and comfortable”). この曲は優しくて落ち着きます (“This piece is gentle and calming”). 綺麗→綺麗で (な-adjective); 優しい→優しくて (い-adjective).

Speaking practice: say one short sentence before looking at each model; then substitute a different situation.

1. React to hearing someone likes photography, using 〜んですね: 写真が好きなんですね！ (“Oh, you like photography!”)
2. You tried speaking Japanese and are glad you did, using 〜て良かった: 日本語で話しかけて良かったです。 (“I'm glad I approached someone in Japanese.”)
3. Describe a quiet place with friendly people, linking adjectives: この町は静かで、人も親切です。 (“This town is quiet and the people are kind.”)
4. Say it makes you happy when someone encourages you, using 〜てもらえると: 励ましてもらえると嬉しいです。 (“I'm happy when someone encourages me.”)
5. Say you are gradually getting used to something: 新しい生活に少しずつ慣れてきました。 (“I'm gradually getting used to my new life.”)
6. Say piano is fun and a change of pace, using 〜上に: ピアノは楽しい上に、気分転換になります。 (“Piano is fun and a nice change of pace too.”)
